derivations.claim: Regard $B=iA$ as a complex matrix on $\mathbb C^{2N}$. Since $A^{\mathsf T}=-A$ and $A$ is real, $B^*=(-i)A^{\mathsf T}=iA=B$. By [F1], $B$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. Complex conjugation sends an eigenvector of eigenvalue $\epsilon>0$ to an eigenvector of eigenvalue $-\epsilon$, because conjugating $iAz=\epsilon z$ gives $-iA\overline z=\epsilon\overline z$. Thus nonzero eigenvalues occur in opposite pairs.

Fix a unit eigenvector $z=u+iv$ for $\epsilon>0$, with real vectors $u,v$. The vectors $z$ and $\overline z$ belong to distinct eigenspaces of the Hermitian matrix $B$, so $\langle z,\overline z\rangle=0$. Expanding this equality gives $\|u\|^2=\|v\|^2$ and $u\cdot v=0$; $\|z\|=1$ then gives $\|u\|=\|v\|=1/\sqrt2$. From $Az=-i\epsilon z$, comparison of real and imaginary parts gives $Au=\epsilon v$ and $Av=-\epsilon u$. Therefore $e_1=\sqrt2u$ and $e_2=-\sqrt2v$ are orthonormal and $Ae_1=-\epsilon e_2$, $Ae_2=\epsilon e_1$, which is the displayed block in this basis.

Choose an orthonormal basis in each positive eigenspace of $B$; [F1] supplies these finite-dimensional bases. Together with their complex conjugates, the chosen vectors are orthonormal: conjugation preserves orthonormality, and every positive eigenspace is orthogonal to every negative eigenspace of the Hermitian matrix $B$. Hence the real planes from step 2.1 are mutually orthogonal. On the zero eigenspace, $Az=0$, so the real and imaginary parts of each vector lie in the real kernel of $A$. The real and complex kernels have equal dimension because row reduction of the real matrix $A$ has the same pivots over $\mathbb R$ and $\mathbb C$; this dimension is $2N$ minus twice the total number of positive eigenvectors, hence even. Choose a real basis of $\ker A$ and successively subtract projections onto earlier vectors and normalize each nonzero residual; this gives an orthonormal real basis. Pairing consecutive vectors gives zero blocks. The resulting real orthonormal basis gives the required $O$.

Since $O$ is orthogonal, $(OAO^{\mathsf T})^{\mathsf T}(OAO^{\mathsf T})=OA^{\mathsf T}AO^{\mathsf T}=\bigoplus_{r=1}^N\epsilon_r^2I_2$. Thus the singular-value multiset from the Statement has two entries $\epsilon_r$ for each block $r$, including its two zero entries when $\epsilon_r=0$. This identifies every positive block value once per real two-plane and completes the multiplicity assertion.

derivations.claim: For every site, $\gamma_{2j-1}\gamma_{2j}=X_jY_j=iZ_j$, so $ih\gamma_{2j-1}\gamma_{2j}=-hZ_j$. For $j<N$, $\gamma_{2j}\gamma_{2j+1}=Y_jZ_jX_{j+1}=iX_jX_{j+1}$, so $iJ\gamma_{2j}\gamma_{2j+1}=-JX_jX_{j+1}$. Summing exactly these terms gives the open-chain $H_N$ of [F1], with no $j=N$ bond.

For any paired indices $a<b$ with coefficient $c$, setting $(A_N)_{ab}=2c$ and $(A_N)_{ba}=-2c$ contributes $(i/4)(2c\gamma_a\gamma_b-2c\gamma_b\gamma_a)=ic\gamma_a\gamma_b$ by [F2]. Applying this to $c=h$ on $(2j-1,2j)$ and $c=J$ on $(2j,2j+1)$ yields $H_N=(i/4)\gamma^{\mathsf T}A_N\gamma$.

By [F3], choose a real orthogonal $O$ with $OA_NO^{\mathsf T}$ in the displayed $2\times2$ blocks, and put $\eta=O\gamma$. Since $O$ is real and orthogonal, [F2] gives $\{\eta_a,\eta_b\}=2\delta_{ab}I$. Define $b_r=(\eta_{2r-1}+i\eta_{2r})/2$. Direct expansion using these anticommutators gives $\{b_r,b_s^*\}=\delta_{rs}I$, $\{b_r,b_s\}=0$, and $b_r^*b_r=\tfrac12I+\tfrac{i}{2}\eta_{2r-1}\eta_{2r}$. Using the matrix expression from step 2.1, substitution into the block expression gives $H_N=\sum_r\epsilon_r(b_r^*b_r-\tfrac12I)$.

The projections $n_r=b_r^*b_r$ commute by the CAR in step 3.1 and are simultaneously diagonalizable: diagonalize $n_1$ using [F5], restrict the remaining commuting Hermitian matrices to its invariant eigenspaces, and continue through the finite list. Their joint eigenvalues lie in $\{0,1\}^N$. If a joint eigenspace has occupancy $0$ in coordinate $r$, $b_r^*$ maps it isometrically into the eigenspace with that bit changed to $1$, since $\|b_r^*\psi\|^2=\langle\psi,(I-n_r)\psi\rangle=\|\psi\|^2$; when the bit is $1$, $b_r$ is the inverse isometry. Hence all $2^N$ joint eigenspaces have the same positive dimension. Their orthogonal sum is $\mathcal H_N$, whose dimension is $2^N$, so each eigenspace is one-dimensional. The resulting ordered occupation basis identifies the $b_r$ representation unitarily with the finite fermionic Fock occupation basis.

In that occupation basis, $\sum_r\epsilon_r b_r^*b_r$ is the diagonal finite-mode Hamiltonian with energies $\epsilon_r$. Apply [F4] with mode set $\{1,\ldots,N\}$, chemical potential $0$, and $q_r=e^{-\beta\epsilon_r}$ to obtain trace $\prod_r(1+e^{-\beta\epsilon_r})$. The scalar shift $-\tfrac12\sum_r\epsilon_r I$ multiplies this trace by $e^{\beta\sum_r\epsilon_r/2}$, and [F5] permits the unitary change back to $\mathcal H_N$. Thus $Z_N=\prod_r(e^{\beta\epsilon_r/2}+e^{-\beta\epsilon_r/2})=\prod_r2\cosh(\beta\epsilon_r/2)$. If $\epsilon_r=0$, its factor is $2$.

By [F2] under the explicit Countable Choice hypothesis [A1], the scalar Fourier-coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry from the complete space $L^2(\mathbb T)$ of [F3] onto scalar $\ell^2(\mathbb Z;\mathbb C)$, with inverse given by the finite-subset-net Fourier series. Applying this to each of the two coordinates proves completeness of $\ell^2(\mathbb Z;\mathbb C^2)$ with [F1]'s norm. The inverse Fourier map applied coordinatewise is a unitary and agrees with $\mathcal F_0$ on finitely supported sequences by its finite polynomial formula. citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $N\ge1$ be an integer and let $\mathcal H_N=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes N}$ with the product inner product linear in its first argument. At each factor use
$$
X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad I_2=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$
For $1\le j\le N$, $X_j,Y_j,Z_j$ denote these matrices on factor $j$ and $I_2$ on every other factor. For real $h,J$ measured in joules define the finite open-chain matrix
$$H_N(h,J)=-h\sum_{j=1}^N Z_j-J\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}X_jX_{j+1}.$$
The upper limit $N-1$ is the open-boundary convention: no term couples site $N$ to site $1$. Put $S_0=I_{\mathcal H_N}$ and $S_{j-1}=Z_1\cdots Z_{j-1}$ for $j>1$. The ordered Majorana operators are
$$\gamma_{2j-1}=S_{j-1}X_j,\qquad \gamma_{2j}=S_{j-1}Y_j\qquad(1\le j\le N).$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $N\ge1$, use the open-chain Hilbert space and Hamiltonian $H_N(h,J)$ of the ordered Majorana definition, and let $\beta>0$ have units $\mathrm{J}^{-1}$ while $h,J$ have units joules. Define the real skew matrix $A_N\in M_{2N}(\mathbb R)$ by $ (A_N)_{2j-1,2j}=2h$ for $1\le j\le N$, $(A_N)_{2j,2j+1}=2J$ for $1\le j<N$, the opposite entries by skew-symmetry, and all other entries by zero. Let $\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_N\ge0$ be its real orthogonal block energies, including zero values. Then
$$H_N(h,J)=\frac{i}{4}\gamma^{\mathsf T}A_N\gamma=\sum_{r=1}^N\epsilon_r\left(b_r^*b_r-\frac12I\right)$$
for the transformed Majorana modes $b_r$ in the Proof, and its finite Gibbs trace is
$$Z_N(\beta;h,J):=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal H_N}(e^{-\beta H_N(h,J)})=\prod_{r=1}^N2\cosh\!\left(\frac{\beta\epsilon_r}{2}\right).$$
Every zero mode contributes a factor two. The chain is open throughout; no periodic Jordan–Wigner parity boundary term is included.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\mathbb T=\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$ and let $m_{\mathbb T}$ be its normalized Borel probability measure, so in the angle coordinate its integral is $\int_{\mathbb T}F\,dm_{\mathbb T}=\int_0^{2\pi}F(k)\,dk/(2\pi)$, obtained from the normalized one-dimensional torus by $k=2\pi x$. On $\mathbb C^2$ use $\langle u,v\rangle_{\mathbb C^2}=u_1\overline{v_1}+u_2\overline{v_2}$ and $\|u\|_{\mathbb C^2}^2=|u_1|^2+|u_2|^2$, linear in the first argument. Define
$$\ell^2(\mathbb Z;\mathbb C^2):=\left\{x=(x_j)_{j\in\mathbb Z}:x_j\in\mathbb C^2,\ \sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}\|x_j\|_{\mathbb C^2}^2<\infty\right\},\quad \langle x,y\rangle_{\ell^2}:=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}\langle x_j,y_j\rangle_{\mathbb C^2}.$$
Define $L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C^2)$ to be the vector space of pairs of Borel-measurable functions $f=(f_1,f_2):\mathbb T\to\mathbb C^2$ with $\int_{\mathbb T}(|f_1|^2+|f_2|^2)\,dm_{\mathbb T}<\infty$, modulo equality $m_{\mathbb T}$-almost everywhere, with inner product
$$\langle f,g\rangle_{L^2}:=\int_{\mathbb T}\bigl(f_1\overline{g_1}+f_2\overline{g_2}\bigr)\,dm_{\mathbb T}.$$
These pairings are linear in the first argument. The square-summable-family supplier gives the scalar $\ell^2$ norm and pairing used coordinatewise. The $L^2$ space is the pair of scalar $L^2$ quotient spaces with the displayed sum inner product and completeness convention. Let $c_{00}(\mathbb Z;\mathbb C^2):=\{x\in\ell^2(\mathbb Z;\mathbb C^2):\{j:x_j\ne0\}\text{ is finite}\}$. Define the linear map
$$\mathcal F_0x(k)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}x_j e^{ijk},\qquad k\in\mathbb T,$$
componentwise, from $c_{00}(\mathbb Z;\mathbb C^2)$ to $L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C^2)$. Its values are continuous finite sums and therefore belong to this $L^2$ space. Then $\mathcal F_0$ preserves inner products on finitely supported sequences and has a unique extension to a surjective linear isometry (a unitary map) $\mathcal F:\ell^2(\mathbb Z;\mathbb C^2)\to L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C^2)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\mathbb T=\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$ and let $m_{\mathbb T}$ be its normalized Borel probability measure, so in the angle coordinate its integral is $\int_{\mathbb T}F\,dm_{\mathbb T}=\int_0^{2\pi}F(k)\,dk/(2\pi)$, obtained from the normalized one-dimensional torus by $k=2\pi x$. On $\mathbb C^2$ use $\langle u,v\rangle_{\mathbb C^2}=u_1\overline{v_1}+u_2\overline{v_2}$ and $\|u\|_{\mathbb C^2}^2=|u_1|^2+|u_2|^2$, linear in the first argument. Define
$$\ell^2(\mathbb Z;\mathbb C^2):=\left\{x=(x_j)_{j\in\mathbb Z}:x_j\in\mathbb C^2,\ \sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}\|x_j\|_{\mathbb C^2}^2<\infty\right\},\quad \langle x,y\rangle_{\ell^2}:=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}\langle x_j,y_j\rangle_{\mathbb C^2}.$$
Define $L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C^2)$ to be the vector space of pairs of Borel-measurable functions $f=(f_1,f_2):\mathbb T\to\mathbb C^2$ with $\int_{\mathbb T}(|f_1|^2+|f_2|^2)\,dm_{\mathbb T}<\infty$, modulo equality $m_{\mathbb T}$-almost everywhere, with inner product
$$\langle f,g\rangle_{L^2}:=\int_{\mathbb T}\bigl(f_1\overline{g_1}+f_2\overline{g_2}\bigr)\,dm_{\mathbb T}.$$
These pairings are linear in the first argument. The square-summable-family supplier gives the scalar $\ell^2$ norm and pairing used coordinatewise. The $L^2$ space is the pair of scalar $L^2$ quotient spaces with the displayed sum inner product and completeness convention. Let $c_{00}(\mathbb Z;\mathbb C^2):=\{x\in\ell^2(\mathbb Z;\mathbb C^2):\{j:x_j\ne0\}\text{ is finite}\}$. Define the linear map
$$\mathcal F_0x(k)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}x_j e^{ijk},\qquad k\in\mathbb T,$$
componentwise, from $c_{00}(\mathbb Z;\mathbb C^2)$ to $L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C^2)$. Its values are continuous finite sums and therefore belong to this $L^2$ space. Then $\mathcal F_0$ preserves inner products on finitely supported sequences and has a unique extension to a surjective linear isometry (a unitary map) $\mathcal F:\ell^2(\mathbb Z;\mathbb C^2)\to L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C^2)$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A $\mathbb K$-linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and $T$ a linear operator on $H$ with domain $D(T)$. Write $(z-T)x=zx-Tx$ for $x\in D(T)$. The **resolvent set**
of $T$ is
$$\rho(T):=\{z\in\mathbb C:\ z-T:D(T)\to H\text{ is bijective and }(z-T)^{-1}\in\mathcal B(H)\},$$
where $\mathcal B(H)$ is the space of bounded everywhere defined operators on
$H$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]); the **spectrum** is
$\sigma(T):=\mathbb C\setminus\rho(T)$. For $z\in\rho(T)$ the bounded operator
$$R_T(z):=(z-T)^{-1}\in\mathcal B(H)$$
is the **resolvent** of $T$ at $z$. This is the library convention used
throughout the page, matching the bounded resolvent of
[[def-spectrum-and-resolvent-of-a-bounded-operator]]: the shift is $zI-T$, with coefficient $-1$ on $T$.

**The resolvent determines $T$ back.** If $z\in\rho(T)$ and $R:=R_T(z)$, then
$D(T)=\operatorname{ran}R$ and $TRy=zRy-y$ for $y\in H$; equivalently
$T=zI-R^{-1}$ with $D(T)=\operatorname{ran}R$, and $R(z-T)x=x$ for
$x\in D(T)$, $(z-T)Ry=y$ for $y\in H$.

**Nonempty resolvent set forces closedness, without the closed graph
theorem.** Assume $\rho(T)\ne\varnothing$ and fix $z\in\rho(T)$ with
$R:=R_T(z)$. Choose a bound $C\ge0$ such that $\|Rv\|\le C\|v\|$.
The map $F(v,w)=w-Rv$ is continuous, since
$\|F(v,w)-F(v',w')\|\le\|w-w'\|+C\|v-v'\|$.
Its zero set $\Gamma(R)=F^{-1}(\{0\})$ is closed. Because
$D(T)=\operatorname{ran}R$ and $(z-T)Rv=v$ for every $v\in H$, the graph of $T$ is
$$\Gamma(T)=\{(x,Tx):x\in D(T)\}=\{(Rv,zRv-v):v\in H\}=\Phi(\Gamma(R)),$$
where $\Phi(v,w):=(w,zw-v)$ is a continuous linear bijection of $H\oplus H$ with
continuous inverse $\Psi(u,v)=(zu-v,u)$, since $\Phi(\Psi(u,v))=(u,z u-(zu-v))=(u,v)$
and $\Psi(\Phi(v,w))=\Psi(w,zw-v)=(v,w)$. A homeomorphism carries closed sets
to closed sets, so $\Gamma(T)$ is closed and $T$ is closed.
No closed graph theorem and hence no choice principle is used here.

For the zero operator on a nonzero $H$, $\rho(0)=\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$: the nonzero shifts have inverse $z^{-1}I$, whereas the zero shift is not bijective. If $H=\{0\}$, every shift is the unique bijection of the zero space, so $\rho(T)=\mathbb C$ and $\sigma(T)=\varnothing$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map

$$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$

is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with

$$\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for every }x\in H .$$

The **Hilbert adjoint** of $T$ is the map

$$T^*:K\longrightarrow H,\qquad y\longmapsto T^*y .$$

It is the unique map $K\to H$ satisfying the displayed identity, since two such maps have $\langle x,(T^*_1-T^*_2)y\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and hence $(T^*_1-T^*_2)y=0$ by positive definiteness.

**The dictionary with the Banach transpose.** Write $R_H:H\to H^*$ and $R_K:K\to K^*$ for the Riesz maps $R_H(x)=\langle\,\cdot\,,x\rangle_H$ and $R_K(y)=\langle\,\cdot\,,y\rangle_K$, and let $T'\in\mathcal B(K^*,H^*)$ be the transpose of $T$, $(T'g)(x)=g(Tx)$ ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then for all $y\in K$ and $x\in H$,

$$\bigl(R_H(T^*y)\bigr)(x)=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H=\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=(R_Ky)(Tx)=\bigl(T'(R_Ky)\bigr)(x),$$

so $R_H\,T^*=T'\,R_K$. The Hilbert adjoint is thus the Banach transpose conjugated by the Riesz identifications of $H$ and $K$ with their duals; it is a different operator from $T'$ whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear.

Throughout, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^n$ is written
$\lambda_n$ ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]), and
$\mathbb Z\subseteq\mathbb R$ is the copy of the integers
([[def-integers]]).

**The torus.** Let $q:\mathbb R\to\mathbb T:=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be the
canonical projection of the quotient of the additive group $\mathbb R$ by its
subgroup $\mathbb Z$, carrying the quotient topology
([[def-quotient-topology]], [[def-topological-space]]); we write
$[t]:=q(t)=t+\mathbb Z$. Thus $[s]=[t]$ exactly when $s-t\in\mathbb Z$. The map
$q$ is continuous ([[def-continuous-map-top]]), and $\mathbb T$ is a compact
Hausdorff space homeomorphic to the Euclidean unit circle.

**Fundamental domain.** Every class has exactly one representative in $[0,1)$:
for $t\in\mathbb R$ the integer part $n=\lfloor t\rfloor$ satisfies
$n\le t<n+1$, so $t-n\in[0,1)$ represents $[t]$ ([[lem-integer-part]]); and if
$s,t\in[0,1)$ satisfy $s-t\in\mathbb Z$, then $|s-t|<1$ forces $s=t$.
Consequently the map $[0,1)\to\mathbb T$, $t\mapsto[t]$, is a bijection.

**Topological checks.** The closed interval $[0,1]$ is compact by [[thm-heine-borel-r]] and maps onto $\mathbb T$, so the quotient is compact by [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]. The map $t\mapsto(\cos 2\pi t,\sin 2\pi t)$ is continuous by [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]] and [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]], and is constant on quotient fibres by [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]]. It induces a continuous map $\varphi:\mathbb T\to S^1$ by [[thm-quotient-universal-property]]. The bijection of $[0,2\pi)$ with the circle in [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]], together with the unique representatives in $[0,1)$, makes $\varphi$ bijective. The Euclidean circle is Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]], so the compact-to-Hausdorff clause of [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]] makes $\varphi$ a homeomorphism. In particular $\mathbb T$ is Hausdorff.

The map $q$ is open: for an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R$, its saturation $q^{-1}[q[U]]=\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb Z}(U+k)$ is open. The images under $q$ of rational-endpoint open intervals form a countable base: if $q(t)\in V$ with $V$ open, choose such an interval containing $t$ and contained in $q^{-1}[V]$. Its image is an open neighbourhood contained in $V$.

**The measure.** For a Borel set $E\in\mathcal B(\mathbb T)$
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) the preimage $q^{-1}[E]$ is a Borel subset of
$\mathbb R$, because $q$ is continuous
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]), hence Lebesgue
measurable ([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). Define

$$m_{\mathbb T}(E):=\lambda_1\bigl(q^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1)\bigr) ,$$

the value at $q^{-1}[E]$ of the same-ambient restriction of $\lambda_1$ to $[0,1)$
([[def-restriction-of-a-measure]]).

This is a measure on $\mathcal B(\mathbb T)$ by [[prop-restriction-is-a-measure]]:
the assignment $E\mapsto\lambda_1(q^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1))$ is the composition of the
restriction measure with the inverse image along $q$, and inverse images preserve
the empty set, complements and countable unions, while countable additivity is
that of $\lambda_1$. It is a **probability measure**:
$m_{\mathbb T}(\mathbb T)=\lambda_1([0,1))=1$
([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]). Thus
$(\mathbb T,\mathcal B(\mathbb T),m_{\mathbb T})$ is a probability measure space
([[def-measure-space]], [[def-measure]]).

**The integral.** For a Borel measurable $F:\mathbb T\to[0,+\infty]$, define

$$\int_{\mathbb T}F\,dm_{\mathbb T}:=\int_{[0,1)}F\circ q\,d\lambda_1 .$$

The defining integral is meaningful because $F\circ q$ is Borel
([[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]],
[[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]). The assignment agrees with
$E\mapsto m_{\mathbb T}(E)$ on indicators, and it is additive and homogeneous on
finite nonnegative simple functions; for a sequence $0\le F_0\le F_1\le\cdots$
with $F_n\uparrow F$ pointwise the identity passes to the limit because
$F_n\circ q\uparrow F\circ q$ and monotone convergence holds for $\lambda_1$
([[thm-increasing-simple-approximation-of-a-nonnegative-measurable-function]],
[[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]). For real or complex integrable
$F$ the integral is defined by decomposition into nonnegative parts or into real
and imaginary parts, and it is linear
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]],
[[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]). In particular
$\int_{\mathbb T}1\,dm_{\mathbb T}=1$, and the same formula holds with $[0,1)$
replaced by any half-open interval $[a,a+1)$ or $(a,a+1]$, by the periodicity of
$q^{-1}[E]$ and the translation invariance of $\lambda_1$
([[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]).

**Translation invariance.** For $y\in\mathbb R$ the map
$\tau_y:\mathbb T\to\mathbb T$, $\tau_y([t]):=[t+y]$, is well defined (if
$s-t\in\mathbb Z$ then $(s+y)-(t+y)\in\mathbb Z$) and continuous, because it is
induced by the continuous map $t\mapsto q(t+y)$ from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb T$. This composite is constant on the fibres of $q$, since $q(t)=q(s)$ implies $q(t+y)=q(s+y)$ ([[thm-quotient-universal-property]]). It preserves
$m_{\mathbb T}$: write $y=n+r$ with $n=\lfloor y\rfloor$ and $r\in[0,1)$, put
$A:=q^{-1}[E]$ and use that $A-n=A$ and that
$A\cap[0,1)=\bigl(A\cap[0,r)\bigr)\cup\bigl(A\cap[r,1)\bigr)$ while
$A\cap[r,r+1)=\bigl(A\cap[r,1)\bigr)\cup\bigl((A\cap[0,r))+1\bigr)$, so that

$$m_{\mathbb T}(\tau_y^{-1}E)=\lambda_1\bigl((A-y)\cap[0,1)\bigr)=\lambda_1\bigl(A\cap[r,r+1)\bigr)=\lambda_1\bigl(A\cap[0,1)\bigr)=m_{\mathbb T}(E),$$

the middle equality by translation invariance of $\lambda_1$. Hence
$(\mathbb T,\mathcal B(\mathbb T),m_{\mathbb T},\tau_y)$ is a measure-preserving
system for every $y$, and the published integral-invariance theorem gives
$\int_{\mathbb T}F\circ\tau_y\,dm_{\mathbb T}=\int_{\mathbb T}F\,dm_{\mathbb T}$
for every measurable $F\ge0$ and every integrable $F$
([[def-measure-preserving-transformation-and-system]],
[[thm-integrals-are-invariant-under-measure-preserving-maps]]). This is the
**normalized Haar integral** of $\mathbb T$; abstract Haar theory is not
invoked.

**The finite torus.** For a natural $n\ge1$ put
$\mathbb T^n:=\mathbb R^n/\mathbb Z^n$ with the quotient topology of the
canonical projection $q_n$, and define

$$m_{\mathbb T^n}(E):=\lambda_n\bigl(q_n^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1)^n\bigr),\qquad \int_{\mathbb T^n}F\,dm_{\mathbb T^n}:=\int_{[0,1)^n}F\circ q_n\,d\lambda_n .$$

Coordinatewise integer parts give unique representatives in $[0,1)^n$, and the continuous quotient map sends the compact cube $[0,1]^n$ onto $\mathbb T^n$. Compactness of the cube follows from [[thm-heine-borel-r]] and [[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]], and compactness of its image follows from [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]. Preimages of Borel sets are Borel; disjoint preimages and countable additivity make the displayed set function a measure, and the box formula gives total mass one. The integral identity follows from indicators, increasing simple approximation and decomposition exactly as in one dimension. For translation invariance, discard the integer parts of the translation vector, split each coordinate of $[0,1)^n$ at its fractional part, and translate the resulting $2^n$ disjoint half-open boxes by integer vectors to partition the translated cube. The periodic preimage set is unchanged by these integer vectors; finite additivity and Lebesgue translation invariance give the same measure. Applying the indicator identity, simple approximation and decomposition gives the integral formula on any translated cube. The coordinate projections induce a continuous bijection
$\Phi:\mathbb T^n\to(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^n$ by the universal property. Its
domain is compact by the preceding check, while its codomain is a finite
product of Hausdorff spaces and hence Hausdorff ([[lem-products-preserve-t0-t1-and-hausdorff]]); the continuous-bijection
theorem therefore makes $\Phi$ a homeomorphism. Thus $\mathbb T^n$ carries the
finite product topology ([[def-product-topology]],
[[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]],
[[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), and its characters
$x\mapsto\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, are defined on this compact
Hausdorff space: replacing representatives by integer vectors leaves the exponential unchanged by [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] and the trigonometric period. Finite products of the countable base above form a countable rectangular base. Hence every product-open set is a countable union of Borel rectangles. Conversely coordinate projections are continuous, so Borel rectangles are Borel in the product. Thus the product Borel sigma-algebra equals the Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb T^n$. On a product $A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1}$ of Borel subsets
of the factors, the defining fundamental-domain formula and repeated application of [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]] give
$m_{\mathbb T^n}(A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1})=\prod_jm_{\mathbb T}(A_j)$, so
$m_{\mathbb T^n}$ agrees on every measurable rectangle with the product measure
$m_{\mathbb T}\times\cdots\times m_{\mathbb T}$
([[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]]); both are probability measures,
and uniqueness of the product measure on sigma-finite spaces identifies them
on the entire Borel sigma-algebra
([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]).
Fubini's theorem then computes iterated integrals of $L^1$ functions on
$\mathbb T^n$
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

derivations.claim: Let $S_+f$ have coordinates $(S_+f)_j=f_{j+1}$ and let $S_-f$ have $(S_-f)_j=f_{j-1}$. Reindexing gives $\|S_\pm f\|=\|f\|$ and $\langle S_-f,g\rangle=\langle f,S_+g\rangle$, so $S_-^*=S_+$ and $S_+^*=S_-$ by [F6]. The Fourier-unitarity fact [F2] makes $\mathcal K$ a Hilbert space, so the bounded shifts and their bounded linear combinations have Hilbert adjoints under [F6]. With $B=2hI-2JS_-$, $B^*=2hI-2JS_+$; the block formula $A_\infty=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&B\\-B^*&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ then gives $A_\infty^*=-A_\infty$. By [F3] and the triangle inequality, both $B$ and $B^*$ have bound $2(|h|+|J|)$, whence $\|A_\infty x\|^2=\|Bv\|^2+\|B^*u\|^2\le4(|h|+|J|)^2\|x\|^2$. Thus $A_\infty$ and $K_\infty=iA_\infty$ are everywhere-defined bounded operators by [F4]. Finally $\langle iA_\infty x,y\rangle=i\langle x,A_\infty^*y\rangle=\langle x,-iA_\infty^*y\rangle$, so $K_\infty^*=-iA_\infty^*=iA_\infty=K_\infty$ by [F6].

For a finitely supported sequence, $\mathcal F(v_{j-1})(k)=e^{ik}\widehat v(k)$ and $\mathcal F(u_{j+1})(k)=e^{-ik}\widehat u(k)$ by reindexing the sums. Therefore $\mathcal F A_\infty\mathcal F^{-1}$ is multiplication by $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&2(h-Je^{ik})\\-2(h-Je^{-ik})&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$; boundedness and density extend the identity to all of $\ell^2$. Multiplication by $i$ gives the displayed $M(k)$.

Put $a(k)=2i(h-Je^{ik})$. Then $M(k)=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&a(k)\\\overline{a(k)}&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ and $M(k)^2=|a(k)|^2I$. Its characteristic polynomial is $\lambda^2-|a(k)|^2$, so its two eigenvalues are $\pm|a(k)|=\pm2\sqrt{h^2+J^2-2hJ\cos k}$, including the double zero when $a(k)=0$.

Let $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ lie outside the union of the two bands in the Statement. By step 3.1, $\epsilon(k)=|a(k)|$ for every $k$, so $d(k):=|\lambda^2-|a(k)|^2|$ is continuous and strictly positive on $\mathbb T$. For each $k_0$, the open set $U_{k_0}:=\{k:d(k)>d(k_0)/2\}$ contains $k_0$. Compactness from [F7] supplies a finite subcover $U_{k_1},\ldots,U_{k_m}$, whence $d(k)>c:=\min_{1\le r\le m}d(k_r)/2>0$ for every $k$. The matrix identity $(M(k)-\lambda I)(M(k)+\lambda I)=(|a(k)|^2-\lambda^2)I$ therefore gives the pointwise inverse $(M(k)+\lambda I)/(|a(k)|^2-\lambda^2)$. This inverse matrix field is continuous and its operator norm is uniformly bounded because $\|M(k)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le2(|h|+|J|)$ and $d(k)\ge c$. Multiplication by it is an everywhere-defined bounded two-sided inverse for $\mathsf M-\lambda I$, and its negative is an inverse for $\lambda I-\mathsf M$. Conjugating by $\mathcal F$ puts $\lambda$ in the resolvent of $K_\infty$ by [F5]. Thus the spectrum is contained in the two bands.

Fix $k_0\in\mathbb T$. When $a(k_0)\ne0$, the vectors $w_+=(a(k_0)/|a(k_0)|,1)/\sqrt2$ and $w_-=(-a(k_0)/|a(k_0)|,1)/\sqrt2$ are unit eigenvectors of $M(k_0)$ with eigenvalues $\pm\epsilon(k_0)$ by step 3.1; when $a(k_0)=0$, $M(k_0)=0$ and either standard unit vector is an eigenvector. For either eigenvalue $\lambda$, set $\delta_n=\min(\pi/2,1/n)$ and let $I_n=\{k_0+[t]:-\delta_n<t<\delta_n\}$, an open arc of angular length $2\delta_n$ and measure $m_{\mathbb T}(I_n)=\delta_n/\pi>0$ by [F7]. Put $\psi_n(k)=\mathbf1_{I_n}(k)w/\sqrt{m_{\mathbb T}(I_n)}$ using the corresponding fixed eigenvector $w$. Then $\|\psi_n\|_2=1$ and continuity of $M$ gives $\|(\mathsf M-\lambda I)\psi_n\|_2\le\sup_{k\in I_n}\|(M(k)-M(k_0))w\|\to0$. If $\mathsf M-\lambda I$ had a bounded inverse, these unit vectors would have residual norms bounded below by the reciprocal inverse norm, a contradiction. By [F5] and the unitary equivalence in step 2.1, every band value lies in the spectrum of $K_\infty$.

Steps 4.1 and 4.2 give both inclusions, so the spectrum is exactly $\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb T}\{-\epsilon(k),\epsilon(k)\}$. Since $\cos k\in[-1,1]$, step 3.1 gives $\min_k\epsilon(k)^2=4(h^2+J^2-2|hJ|)=4(|h|-|J|)^2$. The minimum is attained at $k=0$ when $hJ\ge0$ and at $k=\pi$ when $hJ<0$. Taking the nonnegative square root gives $\Delta_{\mathrm{bulk}}=2\bigl||h|-|J|\bigr|$, which vanishes exactly for $|h|=|J|$. This concerns the one-particle convolution operator only.

risk_review.notes: Read the complete six-step proof and all nine declared direct suppliers. With linear-first inner product the bilateral shifts satisfy S_-*=S_+, B=2hI-2JS_-, and A has block form (0,B;-B*,0), giving the stated boundedness and self-adjoint iA. Positive Fourier exponent sends backward shift to exp(ik), matching M exactly. M^2=|a|^2I gives both eigenvalues including a=0. For every complex lambda outside the bands, compactness gives a positive uniform denominator and the explicit inverse has the correct sign for lambda I-M. For each band value, fixed unit eigenvectors and positive-measure shrinking arcs yield normalized approximate eigenvectors; bounded inverse inequality excludes resolvent membership, including zero and constant bands. No measurable eigenvector selection theorem is assumed. The minimum occurs at 0 for hJ>=0 and pi for hJ<0; hJ=0 gives constant bands, h=J=0 gives {0}, and both directions of gap-zero iff |h|=|J| hold. Countable Choice and torus quotient normalization are retained. Contract citations match the exact current definitions. This is solely the explicitly defined one-particle operator, with no spin-chain infinite-volume ground-state or thermodynamic assertion.

citations.quote: The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following statement.
Assume Countable Choice.
For real $h,J$ measured in joules define the finite open-chain matrix $$H_N(h,J)=-h\sum_{j=1}^N Z_j-J\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}X_jX_{j+1}.$$
its finite Gibbs trace is $$Z_N(\beta;h,J):=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal H_N}(e^{-\beta H_N(h,J)})=\prod_{r=1}^N2\cosh\!\left(\frac{\beta\epsilon_r}{2}\right).$$
Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues.

derivations.claim: At $h=0$, an $X$-basis configuration $s=(s_1,\ldots,s_N)\in\{-1,1\}^N$ has energy $-J\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}s_js_{j+1}$. Each bond contributes at least $-J$, with equality exactly when $s_j=s_{j+1}$. Since the open chain is connected, all bonds attain equality exactly for the two constant configurations; for $N=1$ the empty bond sum leaves its two basis configurations degenerate as well.

At $J=0$, a $Z$-basis configuration $s\in\{-1,1\}^N$ has energy $-h\sum_js_j$. If $h>0$, each site uniquely minimizes its term by taking $s_j=1$; if $h<0$, each site uniquely minimizes its term by taking $s_j=-1$. Thus the unique minimizing $Z$-configuration has the orientation stated in the Example.

For $\beta>0$, [F2] gives the stated product trace for the exact $H_N$ of [F1] and its open-chain energies. The trace itself is the ordinary trace of the finite matrix exponential on the $2^N$-dimensional space.

For an endomorphism $C$ of $\mathcal H_N$, use the operator norm $\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}:=\sup\{\|C\psi\|_{\mathcal H_N}:\|\psi\|_{\mathcal H_N}=1\}$ from the finite product inner product. The entries of $-\beta H_N(h,J)$ are polynomials in $\beta,h,J$. On each compact set of complex parameter triples this matrix has a finite uniform operator-norm bound $C$. Define its complex-parameter exponential by $\exp(-\beta H_N)=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}(-\beta H_N)^m/m!$; the summands have norm at most $C^m/m!$, so the series converges uniformly on each such compact set. The matrix exponential power series is holomorphic in its entries (that is, locally represented by convergent complex power series), so composing it with the polynomial matrix entries makes each matrix entry, and its finite trace, holomorphic in $(\beta,h,J)$. Their restrictions to $\mathbb R^3$ are real-analytic in the sense defined in the Statement. For real parameters, [F3]'s spectral exponential agrees with this series by applying the scalar exponential series to each real eigenvalue $\lambda_r$ of the Hermitian $H_N$; hence $Z_N=\sum_re^{-\beta\lambda_r}>0$. This proves analyticity for each fixed finite $N$ only; it gives no conclusion about the existence or analyticity of a limit as $N\to\infty$.
